source.title: Redundancy and Concept Analysis for Code-trained Language Models
source.authors: Arushi Sharma; Zefu Hu; Christopher J. Quinn; Ali Jannesari

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports qualitative examples of neurons activating for multiple code concepts and explicitly cautions that such patterns may have more than one interpretation. It refines how much can be inferred from polysemantic-looking neurons, but does not test capacity pressure or superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition and defines superposition, but its experiments do not test feature sparsity, capacity competition, overlapping feature directions, or feature dimensionality. Included are its own qualitative multi-concept neuron observations and the authors' stated alternative interpretations. Neuron-removal accuracies, task-probe results, and cited findings are not rows because they do not directly measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper is a neuron-level redundancy and probing study of seven code models. It mentions superposition only to describe a few hand-picked neurons. It gives no measure of capacity, sparsity, feature geometry, SAE recovery or feature dimensionality. Its alternative readings of polysemantic neurons (noise, a higher-level 'text neuron') are suggestions, not tested results. The authors say confirmation 'is either methodologically unfeasible or requires further experiments'. So nothing here bears on whether V3 or any other version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The paper's main conclusions are about redundancy: over 95% of neurons can be removed with little loss in probe accuracy, adjacent layers are similar, and small neuron subsets reach baseline accuracy. On concepts, the authors trace neurons to code properties (number, string and 'text' neurons) and give a few polysemantic-looking examples. They say superposition makes firm conclusions hard and leave its study to future work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses probing, neuron ranking, clustering, and qualitative concept tracing in code-trained language models; it does not reproduce the toy-model feature and geometry experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: not stated for the multi-concept neuron observations

fits_no_version.finding: Qualitative, hand-picked examples of individual neurons in code-trained models that respond to more than one token class (e.g. identifiers and numbers), alongside one fairly clean 'number neuron'. There is no frequency estimate and no causal test.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Code-trained transformers contain both multi-class (polysemantic-looking) and single-class neurons for token types, observed anecdotally via probe-ranked neurons.

record.peer_reviewed: 2024 39th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering Workshops (ASEW)
record.problems: The multi-concept examples are qualitative and limited to selected neurons. They do not causally distinguish superposition from a higher-level concept or noise. The authors also note that concrete mechanistic conclusions are hard to draw and call for further experiments.
record.rows_left_out: None. Other reported task-probe and neuron-reduction results concern task prediction accuracy, not the claim versions' feature-capacity mechanism or representation geometry.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy models, sparsity sweep, phase transition or geometry.
All of it: no test of capacity competition or of important features getting dedicated dimensions.
All of it: non-capacity causes of polysemanticity are suggested (noise, higher-level concept) but not tested.
All of it: no measure of features distributed across many neurons and no sparse dictionary or SAE.
All of it: feature dimensionality is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T5' and 'supports V3' are overreach. The paper defines polysemantic neurons as caused by superposition, and its alternative readings are offhand. The redundancy and correlation-clustering results concern task-relevant information in probes, not superposition, so they were correctly left out as rows.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, feature sparsity, feature-to-dimension ratio, transition behavior, and geometry.
Whether limited capacity causes polysemanticity, and whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
The study does not establish that any observed neuron pattern is caused by a non-superposition mechanism; the alternative explanations are proposed rather than tested.
Whether LLM features are distributed across many neurons or recoverable by sparse autoencoders.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.

rows.subject: CodeBERT
rows.operation_detail: Qualitatively examined concept-associated activations for an individual neuron.
rows.measure: The neuron activates for identifiers and numbers; the authors describe it as polysemantic.
rows.value: Activates for identifiers (negative activation values) and numbers (positive activation values).
rows.note: This shows a multi-concept activation pattern but does not identify its cause; the text presents it as an illustration of polysemanticity.
rows.check: A single hand-picked CodeBERT neuron (L0:47) shown in a visualisation, active for identifiers and numbers. There is no baseline, rate or mechanism test, so it cannot show whether the polysemanticity has a capacity cause or another cause (V2/V3). It is not evidence of features spread across neurons or recoverable by a dictionary (V4).

rows.subject: CodeBERT
rows.operation_detail: Qualitatively examined concept-associated activations for an individual neuron.
rows.measure: The neuron is primarily associated with strings and also highlights a parenthesis.
rows.value: Primarily responsible for strings; also highlights a parenthesis.
rows.note: The authors say this could reflect polysemanticity or noise; neither explanation is experimentally distinguished.
rows.check: An anecdotal CodeBERT neuron (L7:717), mainly active for strings plus one parenthesis. The authors say it might be polysemanticity or noise and test neither.

rows.subject: CodeGPTJava
rows.operation_detail: Qualitatively examined the top words associated with an individual neuron.
rows.measure: Top words and concept associations for the neuron.
rows.value: The neuron is reported as responsible for both keywords and identifiers; listed top words are identity, break, interval, unit, and class.
rows.note: The authors say this could indicate superposition or a higher-level monosemantic 'text neuron'; this study does not determine which interpretation is correct.
rows.check: The CodeGPTJava neuron (L5:305) is shown only by its top-5 words in Table 6. The 'superposition vs. text neuron' reading is speculation and is not tested.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The authors report multi-concept activation patterns but explicitly leave open whether they reflect superposition, a higher-level concept, or noise; the observations therefore do not by themselves establish superposition (r1–r3).
